name: Miriam Makeba
story:
In 1963, Miriam Makeba stood before the United Nations General Assembly and did something no African woman had done before — she testified against apartheid. She was already exiled from South Africa, her passport revoked, her music banned. The regime had erased her from existence back home. She had lost her mother, who died while Miriam was barred from returning. She spoke anyway, her voice steady, describing the brutality her people endured daily. The UN session led to one of the first international resolutions against apartheid.

The cost was staggering. For 31 years, Makeba lived in exile — Guinea, the US, Belgium, wherever would have her. When she married Stokely Carmichael in 1968, the American music industry dropped her overnight. Record deals vanished. Concert venues cancelled. She went from filling Carnegie Hall to being blacklisted across the West. Most artists would have softened their politics to survive. Makeba moved to Guinea and kept singing.

She called herself "not a political person" — she simply sang about the truth of her life, and her life happened to be political. Her song "Pata Pata" made the world dance while her testimony made it think. When Nelson Mandela was finally released in 1990 and invited her home, she walked back into a free South Africa at age 58, having sacrificed her entire prime to a cause she refused to abandon. She performed until days before her death in 2008, collapsing on stage mid-song at a concert against organized crime in Italy — still fighting, still singing, to the very last breath.
